title: Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma (AACG): The Ophthalmological Emergency
summary: AACG represents a true ocular emergency characterized by a rapid, sustained elevation of intraocular pressure due to mechanical obstruction of the trabecular meshwork by the peripheral iris. Immediate recognition and intervention are critical to prevent permanent optic nerve damage and blindness.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: AACG is defined by the sudden apposition of the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork (TM), causing acute outflow obstruction. The primary mechanism is pupillary block (relative resistance to aqueous flow between the lens and iris), leading to iris bombe and angle closure. Secondary causes include plateau iris, phacomorphic glaucoma, or tractional mechanisms.

sections.title: Clinical Features (The 5 'P's)
content: Pain: Severe, boring ocular/periorbital pain.
Pupil: Mid-dilated, non-reactive.
Pressure: Often > 50 mmHg.
Prostration: Nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis.
Perception: Blurred vision with halos around lights.

sections.title: Red Flags (Emergency Signs)
content: Corneal Edema (hazy view)
Fixed mid-dilated pupil
Shallow anterior chamber (Van Herick Grade 1)
Glaukomflecken (anterior subcapsular lens opacities)
Nausea/Vomiting (often misdiagnosed as GI event)

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Assess AC depth, corneal edema, iris position).
Step 2: Tonometry (Goldmann Applanation or Tono-Pen).
Step 3: Gonioscopy (The Gold Standard - assess TM pigmentation and synechiae).
Step 4: Fundoscopy (Evaluate C/D ratio if view allows; check for disc edema).
Step 5: UBM or Anterior Segment OCT (Assess angle anatomy).

sections.title: Management Protocol
content: Immediate: Topical Beta-blockers, Alpha-agonists, Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors.
Systemic: Oral or IV Acetazolamide (500mg), Hyperosmotic agents (Mannitol/Glycerol).
Miotics: Pilocarpine 1-2% (once pressure < 40 mmHg).
Definitive: Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI) or surgical peripheral iridectomy.

content.explanation: C: Corneal edema, A: A-chamber shallow, M: Mid-dilated pupil, P: Pressure high.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Never perform LPI on a hazy cornea; use topical glycerin to clear it.
Always examine the fellow eye; 50% risk of closure in 5 years.
Avoid pilocarpine in high pressure as it is ineffective due to iris ischemia.
